name: Blue-light glasses

lead: Blue-light glasses filter some short-wavelength light from screens and LEDs. They come in clear lenses and fashion frames, and are sold for eye strain and sleep; appearance forums wear them hoping for brighter, less tired-looking eyes.

Tints or coatings reduce transmission of blue light, which is thought to affect comfort and the body clock. Reviews report little support for eye-strain relief, and studies exist in sleep disorders and Parkinson disease. The brighter-eyes claim has not been tested.

paras: People wear them during screen use or in the evening, and many choose them as frames for a styled look. Some wear them in the hours before bed.
Minimal risks are described. Tinted lenses can alter colour perception.

social.title: Research finds that blue-light glasses improve sleep and workday productivity

angle.text: Wearers hope that filtering screen light means less strain and better sleep, and so brighter, less tired-looking eyes, while the frames add to the styled look. Reviews of eye strain relief report little support, and the brighter-eyes effect has not been studied.

lead: Blue-light glasses, also called blue-blocking or blue-filtering glasses, are spectacles with lenses that filter part of the blue end of visible light emitted by screens and LED lighting. They are sold over the counter, often with clear lenses and fashion frames, and marketed for digital eye strain and sleep. In appearance forums they are also claimed to make eyes look brighter or less tired.[1][2]

Reviews summarised on Wikipedia found little support for blue-blocking glasses in digital eye strain, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology, as described by Grokipedia, does not recommend them for it. Studies of blue-light glasses in sleep disorders and in Parkinson disease exist, but no study has tested them for making the eyes look brighter.[2][1][3][4]
infobox: Digital eye strain, sleep, general eye comfort

paras: Lenses may use tints, pigments or coatings that reduce transmission of short-wavelength light by amounts that Grokipedia places at roughly 10 to 25% for common consumer products. Manufacturers' claims, such as filtering specified multiples or percentages of blue light, are statements by the companies rather than independent findings.[2]

Wikipedia's article on computer vision syndrome reports that a 2021 review, published in 2022, found little support for blue-blocking glasses for digital eye strain, and that double-blind trials found no evidence that blue-filter lenses help it. It also notes an earlier amber-lens study that a follow-up did not reproduce, and a lens-industry-sponsored study in which most participants could not detect changes.[1]

Grokipedia describes mixed evidence: a self-reported questionnaire study suggesting benefit, a reported limited short-term effect, and statements from the American Academy of Ophthalmology that digital eye strain stems mainly from reduced blinking and that blue light from devices is not known to damage the eyes. Grokipedia is AI-generated and its account of these reviews contains internal inconsistencies.[2]

For sleep, a 2022 study in 15 patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder used glasses emitting blue light of about 470 nm in the morning, which is a different use from blue-blocking lenses.[3] A 2019 survey examined patient experience with blue-light glasses in Parkinson disease ahead of formal efficacy trials.[4]
A 2023 cross-sectional survey of undergraduate and medical students at one university examined the prevalence of computer vision syndrome after the move to online learning.[5]

Small studies cover blue-light glasses for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder and for Parkinson disease, and reviews cited above assess blue-blocking lenses for digital eye strain with limited support.[1][3][4] No studies found testing blue-light glasses for making the eyes look brighter or less red.
Grokipedia reports that clinical reviews describe minimal risks and that claims of dependency on the glasses lack supporting evidence; it also says tinted lenses can alter colour perception.[2]
